questions.s: Concerning the olfactory pathway, as described in Last's:
o: The first neurons are bipolar cells scattered in the neuroepithelium

Last's describes the first olfactory neurons as bipolar cells scattered among the supporting cells of the olfactory neuroepithelium, and calls a nerve cell body lying in a surface epithelium "a unique occurrence".
Their peripheral processes reach the surface as olfactory hairs; their central processes form the olfactory nerve filaments. (Last's p. 629)
About 40 olfactory nerve filaments pass through the cribriform plate

Last's says "nearly 20" filaments pass through the cribriform plate, not 40.
The number is the trap. Each filament carries a sleeve of meninges through the plate, which is why fractures here cause anosmia and CSF rhinorrhoea. (Last's p. 629)
The filaments pierce the dura and arachnoid of the anterior cranial fossa

The olfactory filaments pass up through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid and pierce the dura and arachnoid of the anterior cranial fossa to reach the olfactory bulb.
This meningeal sleeve is the route by which infection can spread from the nose into the subarachnoid space. (Last's p. 629)
The olfactory tract ends in the region of the posterior perforated substance and the uncus

The olfactory tract ends in the region of the anterior perforated substance and the uncus.
The posterior perforated substance lies between the cerebral peduncles, far behind, and carries branches of the posterior cerebral arteries. "Anterior" is correct here. (Last's p. 629)
The second-order neurons are the mitral cells of the olfactory bulb

The olfactory nerve filaments synapse on the mitral cells of the olfactory bulb, which are the second-order neurons. Their axons form the olfactory tract.
Tufted cells in the bulb also contribute. There are only two neurons from the epithelium to the cortex. (Last's p. 629)
The second-order neuron relays in the thalamus before reaching the cortex

Last's calls the arrangement "primitive": the second-order neuron directly activates the conscious (olfactory) cortex, by-passing the thalamus.
Olfaction is the only sense that reaches its primary cortex without a thalamic relay. (Last's p. 629)
Polysynaptic olfactory pathways activate hypothalamic and brainstem nuclei

Besides the direct path to conscious cortex, polysynaptic olfactory pathways activate hypothalamic and brainstem nuclei, producing visceral and somatic effects (salivation, nausea, changes in gut motility).
These effects are distinct from the conscious appreciation of smell. (Last's p. 629)
Three neurons link the neuroepithelium to the olfactory cortex

Only two neurons link the neuroepithelium to the olfactory cortex: the bipolar receptor cells and the mitral cells.
Other sensory pathways typically need three neurons with a thalamic relay. "Three" is the changed word. (Last's p. 629)

questions.s: Concerning the retina and optic nerve (Last's):
o: The bipolar cells of the retina are the first sensory neurons

In the retina the rods and cones (receptors) activate the bipolar cells, which Last's treats as the first sensory neurons.
The ganglion cells are the second neurons; their axons form the optic nerve. The lateral geniculate body provides the third. (Last's p. 629-30)
The ganglion cells lie on the choroidal surface of the retina

The large ganglion cells lie scattered on the vitreous (inner) surface of the retina. The rods and cones lie near the choroidal (outer) surface.
So light passes through the ganglion and bipolar layers before reaching the receptors. (Last's p. 629-30)
The optic nerve fibres are the central processes of the ganglion cells

The axons (central processes) of the ganglion cells converge on the optic disc and form the optic nerve.
These second-order neurons run without synapse all the way to the lateral geniculate body, pretectal nuclei or superior colliculus. (Last's p. 629-30)
The temporal fibres from each retina decussate in the chiasma

It is the nasal fibres of each retina that decussate in the chiasma. Temporal fibres stay on the same side.
So each optic tract carries the ipsilateral temporal and contralateral nasal fibres, representing the opposite half of the visual field. (Last's p. 629-30)
Crossed nasal fibres relay in layers 2, 3 and 5

Crossed nasal fibres relay in layers 1, 4 and 6 of the lateral geniculate body.
Layers 2, 3 and 5 receive the uncrossed temporal fibres. A memory aid: "crossed = 1, 4, 6". (Last's p. 629-30)
Temporal fibres relay in layers 2, 3 and 5

Uncrossed temporal fibres relay in layers 2, 3 and 5 of the lateral geniculate body.
Crossed nasal fibres take the remaining layers 1, 4 and 6. Each layer therefore receives from only one eye. (Last's p. 629-30)
Third-order fibres leave through the retrolentiform part of the internal capsule

The third-order fibres from the lateral geniculate body leave through the retrolentiform part of the internal capsule and pass back as the optic radiation to the visual cortex.
The retrolentiform part lies behind the lentiform nucleus. (Last's p. 629-30)
Third-order fibres leave through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule

The sublentiform part of the internal capsule carries the auditory radiation (from the medial geniculate body). The optic radiation is retrolentiform.
"Visual behind, auditory below" is the way to remember the two. (Last's p. 629-30)

questions.s: The optic tract and visual cortex:
o: The optic tract passes around the cerebral peduncle

After the chiasma the optic tract winds back around the cerebral peduncle (the lateral side of the midbrain) to reach the lateral geniculate body.
On the way it lies close to the posterior cerebral artery and the uncus. (Last's p. 629-30)
The optic tract has three destinations

The optic tract has three destinations: the lateral geniculate body (vision), the pretectal nuclei (pupillary light reflex) and the superior colliculus (reflex body movements to light).
Most fibres go to the lateral geniculate body. (Last's p. 629-30)
In the visual cortex the macula is represented anteriorly

In the visual cortex the macula is represented posteriorly, near the occipital pole. More peripheral retina registers progressively more anteriorly.
This is why occipital pole lesions cause central (macular) field defects. (Last's p. 629-30)
The superior colliculus fibres mediate pupillary constriction to light

Pupillary constriction to light is mediated by the pretectal nuclei, which project to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei. The superior colliculus serves reflex body (head and eye) movements in response to light.
"Pretectal = pupil" is the rule. (Last's p. 629-30)
Lies at the level of the superior colliculi

The oculomotor nucleus lies at the level of the superior colliculi, in the grey matter in the floor of the aqueduct near the midline.
The trochlear nucleus lies just below, at the level of the inferior colliculi. (Last's p. 630)
Has an Edinger-Westphal part lying caudal to the somatic nucleus

The Edinger–Westphal (accessory oculomotor) nucleus lies cranial to the somatic nucleus, not caudal.
It contains the preganglionic parasympathetic neurons for the pupil and ciliary muscle. (Last's p. 630)
Gives rise to about 24 000 fibres

Last's gives the oculomotor nerve about 24 000 fibres.
Compare the trochlear (about 3400) and abducent (about 6600). The numbers are a favourite "one word changed" trap. (Last's p. 630)
Sends fibres that traverse the brainstem with a medial convexity

The oculomotor fibres traverse the brainstem with a lateral convexity, passing through the red nucleus and substantia nigra to emerge into the interpeduncular fossa.
So a tegmental lesion can damage the fibres and the red nucleus together. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: Concerning the intracranial course of the oculomotor nerve:
o: It is attached to the medial surface of the base of the cerebral peduncle, just above the pons

III emerges from the medial surface of the base of the cerebral peduncle (crus) into the interpeduncular fossa, just above the pons.
Its emergence medially between the peduncles contrasts with IV, which emerges dorsally. (Last's p. 630)
It passes forwards between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries

III runs forward between the posterior cerebral artery (above) and the superior cerebellar artery (below).
This is a classic site: aneurysms or ectatic vessels here can compress the nerve. (Last's p. 630)
It passes above and medial to the posterior communicating artery

III passes below and lateral to the posterior communicating artery.
That close relation is why a posterior communicating aneurysm classically produces a painful III palsy with a dilated pupil. (Last's p. 630)
It runs just above the free margin of the tentorium

III runs just below the free margin of the tentorium cerebelli.
When the uncus herniates over the tentorial edge it compresses III, giving an ipsilateral dilated pupil (Hutchinson's pupil). (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: The oculomotor nerve reaching the cavernous sinus:
o: Traverses the interpeduncular cistern below the floor of the third ventricle

In the interpeduncular cistern III lies below the floor of the third ventricle before reaching the roof of the cavernous sinus.
Lesions distending the third ventricle floor can therefore press on it. (Last's p. 630)
Lies above the optic tract

III lies below the optic tract, not above it.
The optic tract runs back above and lateral to the nerve as it passes forward. (Last's p. 630)
Pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus just behind the upward bend of the internal carotid

III pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus just behind the upward bend of the internal carotid artery, below the optic tract.
It then descends into the lateral wall of the sinus. (Last's p. 630)
Runs a tortuous course with a steep upward slope

Last's says the nerve runs straight with a gentle downward slope from the midbrain to the cavernous sinus.
It is not tortuous and does not slope upward. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: In the cavernous sinus and orbit, the oculomotor nerve:
o: Lies in the lateral wall above the abducent nerve

In the cavernous sinus III lies highest in the lateral wall at first, above VI, which runs in the cavity of the sinus.
It then slopes downward as it goes forward. (Last's p. 630)
Slants down lateral to the trochlear and ophthalmic nerves

III slants down medial to the trochlear nerve and the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal.
As a result, IV becomes the uppermost nerve at the front of the sinus. (Last's p. 630)
Picks up sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus for the smooth muscle part of levator palpebrae superioris

In the sinus III picks up sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus for the smooth muscle part of levator palpebrae superioris (superior tarsal muscle).
Loss of these fibres causes the partial ptosis of Horner's syndrome. (Last's p. 630)
Divides into superior and inferior divisions at the posterior pole of the cavernous sinus

III divides into superior and inferior divisions at the anterior pole of the sinus and immediately enters the tendinous ring.
It runs undivided through the sinus. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: Within the tendinous ring and orbit:
o: The nasociliary nerve lies between the two divisions of the oculomotor nerve

Inside the tendinous ring the nasociliary nerve lies between the superior and inferior divisions of III, with VI below them.
These are the nerves that pass within the ring. Lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves pass above it. (Last's p. 630)
The abducent nerve lies above the oculomotor nerve

VI lies below III within the tendinous ring, not above it.
It then passes to the medial (ocular) surface of lateral rectus. (Last's p. 630)
Each branch enters the ocular surface of its muscle one-third of the way along

Each branch of III enters the ocular surface of its muscle (superior, medial and inferior recti) about one-third of the way along the muscle.
The branch to inferior oblique enters its posterior border instead. (Last's p. 630)
The Edinger-Westphal fibres run in the nerve to medial rectus

The Edinger–Westphal fibres run in the proximal part of the nerve to inferior oblique, from which they pass to the ciliary ganglion.
The nerve to medial rectus carries only somatic motor fibres. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: Regarding the ciliary ganglion connections of the oculomotor nerve:
o: The parasympathetic fibres relay in the ciliary ganglion

Preganglionic fibres from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus relay in the ciliary ganglion.
It is the only type of fibre that synapses there; sympathetic and sensory fibres pass straight through. (Last's p. 630)
The short ciliary nerves supply sphincter pupillae and the ciliary muscle

The postganglionic fibres leave as the short ciliary nerves and supply sphincter pupillae and the ciliary muscle.
They mediate pupillary constriction and accommodation. Dilator pupillae is sympathetic. (Last's p. 630)
The inferior division gives two branches only

The inferior division of III breaks up quickly into three branches: to medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique.
The superior division supplies superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris. (Last's p. 630)
Some afferent fibres passing through the ganglion without relay supply the conjunctiva

Last's says the afferent fibres passing through the ganglion without relay supply the cornea (and the eyeball).
The conjunctiva is supplied by other branches of V1 and V2. The corneal fibres form the afferent limb of the corneal reflex. (Last's p. 630)
The nucleus lies at the level of the inferior colliculi

The trochlear nucleus lies at the level of the inferior colliculi, in the floor of the aqueduct near the midline.
The oculomotor nucleus is above it at the level of the superior colliculi. (Last's p. 630)
The nerve contains about 34 000 fibres

The trochlear nerve contains about 3400 fibres, not 34 000.
It is the smallest cranial nerve. A factor-of-ten change is a common trap. (Last's p. 630)
The fibres decussate completely ventral to the aqueduct

Trochlear fibres decussate completely dorsal to the aqueduct, not ventral.
They cross in the superior medullary velum before emerging. (Last's p. 630)
The nerve emerges through the apex of the superior medullary velum

The trochlear nerve emerges through the apex of the superior medullary velum, dorsally near the midline behind the inferior colliculus.
It is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the dorsal surface of the brainstem. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: Concerning the course of the trochlear nerve:
o: It clings to the under surface of the free edge of the tentorium

IV runs forward clinging to the under surface of the free edge of the tentorium.
That position puts it at risk when the tentorium is incised in surgery. (Last's p. 630)
It pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus behind the oculomotor nerve

IV pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus behind III, where the free and attached margins of the tentorium cross.
Both nerves then descend into the lateral wall. (Last's p. 630)
It runs forwards in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus above the third nerve

IV runs forward in the lateral wall below III. III then crosses it medially, so IV becomes the uppermost nerve at the front of the sinus.
The order changes along the sinus: posteriorly III is above, anteriorly IV is above. (Last's p. 630)
It enters the superior orbital fissure within the tendinous ring

IV enters the orbit lateral to (outside) the tendinous ring and passes over levator palpebrae superioris to superior oblique.
The nerves within the ring are III (both divisions), nasociliary and VI. (Last's p. 630)
Enters the ocular surface of superior oblique

IV enters the orbital (upper) surface of superior oblique, about one-third of the way along the muscle.
The branches of III enter the ocular surfaces of their muscles; IV is the exception. (Last's p. 630)
Becomes the uppermost nerve at the anterior end of the cavernous sinus

Because III crosses medial to it, IV becomes the uppermost nerve at the anterior end of the cavernous sinus.
Posteriorly in the sinus III lies highest. (Last's p. 630)
Passes beneath levator palpebrae superioris in the orbit

IV passes over levator palpebrae superioris, not beneath it, as it crosses medially to superior oblique.
This keeps it outside the muscle cone. (Last's p. 630)
Runs between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries

Like III but more laterally, IV passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.
Both nerves can be compressed by these vessels or by aneurysms at this point. (Last's p. 630)
The motor nucleus is in the upper pons, deep beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle

The trigeminal motor nucleus lies in the upper pons, deep beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle. It is a branchial (special visceral efferent) nucleus for the first-arch muscles, so it lies off centre rather than near the midline.
Compare the somatic motor nuclei (III, IV, VI, XII), which lie close to the midline. (Last's p. 631)
The sensory nuclei extend down to the fifth cervical segment

Last's says the sensory nuclei extend down to the third cervical segment (the upper two or three segments), not the fifth.
Below that the spinal nucleus is continuous with the substantia gelatinosa of the cord. So high cervical lesions can cause facial sensory loss. (Last's p. 631)
The mesencephalic nucleus lies lateral to the aqueduct in the central grey

The mesencephalic nucleus lies lateral to the aqueduct in the central (periaqueductal) grey, running through the whole length of the midbrain.
It is the only nucleus in the CNS made of first-order sensory cell bodies. (Last's p. 631)
The main sensory nucleus lies medial to the motor nucleus

The main (principal) sensory nucleus lies lateral to the motor nucleus, ventral to the superior cerebellar peduncle.
"Motor medial, sensory lateral" holds for the trigeminal nuclei, as it does for most brainstem cranial nerve columns. (Last's p. 631)

questions.s: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal:
o: Contains the cell bodies of first-order neurons

The mesencephalic nucleus contains the cell bodies of first-order (pseudounipolar) neurons. Their peripheral processes pass straight through the trigeminal ganglion without having cell bodies there.
This is unique: it is the only place where primary sensory cell bodies lie inside the CNS rather than in a ganglion. (Last's p. 631)
Mediates proprioception from muscles supplied by the oculomotor, trochlear, abducent and facial nerves

Last's says the mesencephalic nucleus mediates proprioception not only from the muscles of mastication but also from muscles supplied by III, IV, VI and VII (and probably XII).
These proprioceptive fibres reach the trigeminal system through communications in the orbit and face. (Last's p. 631)
Synapses with first-order neurons from the trigeminal ganglion

The cell bodies of the mesencephalic nucleus are themselves the first-order neurons, so they do not synapse with first-order neurons from the trigeminal ganglion.
Their central processes go on to synapse in the motor nucleus (for the jaw jerk) and elsewhere. (Last's p. 631)
Mediates pain and temperature from the face

Pain and temperature from the face are mediated by the spinal trigeminal nucleus.
The mesencephalic nucleus serves proprioception; the main sensory nucleus serves touch. (Last's p. 631)
Extends from the lower pons through the whole medulla

The spinal trigeminal nucleus extends from the lower pons through the whole of the medulla, and is continuous below with the substantia gelatinosa (gelatinous substance) of the upper cervical cord.
This explains facial pain and temperature loss with lateral medullary (PICA) infarction. (Last's p. 631)
Mediates pain and temperature

The spinal nucleus mediates pain and temperature from the face. The main sensory nucleus mediates touch, and the mesencephalic nucleus proprioception.
Each of the three trigeminal sensory nuclei has its own modality. (Last's p. 631)
Is classically said to receive ophthalmic fibres in its uppermost part

The classical description is "upside-down": ophthalmic fibres end in the lowest part of the spinal nucleus, mandibular fibres in the uppermost part.
So V1 fibres descend furthest, which is why they are cut most reliably in medullary tractotomy. (Last's p. 631)
Is shown clinically to have a strictly divisional (V1, V2, V3) pattern

Clinical observations indicate an "onion-skin" pattern, working backwards from the mouth: the area around the mouth is represented highest, and concentric rings further back are represented progressively lower.
A low spinal nucleus lesion therefore causes sensory loss over the back of the face, sparing the area around the mouth. (Last's p. 631)
The sensory root is attached to the pons well lateral and just above centre

The large sensory root of V is attached to the anterolateral pons, well lateral and just above centre.
The motor root emerges just above and medial to it. (Last's p. 631)
The motor root emerges slightly caudal and lateral to the sensory root

The motor root emerges slightly cranial (above) and medial to the sensory root, not caudal and lateral.
It then passes below the ganglion to join the mandibular division. (Last's p. 631)
The roots pass below the tentorium to the mouth of the trigeminal cave

The roots pass forward in the posterior cranial fossa below the tentorium and over the apex of the petrous bone, into the mouth of the trigeminal cave.
At this point they lie under the attached margin of the tentorium, near the superior petrosal sinus. (Last's p. 631)
The cave is a prolongation of dura over the lower border of the petrous apex

The trigeminal cave is a prolongation of dura (and arachnoid) over the upper border of the petrous bone near its apex.
The roots pass over this border from the posterior into the middle fossa, in a notch (the trigeminal impression). (Last's p. 631)
The dural sheath peels apart the two layers of dura flooring the middle fossa

The dural sheath of the trigeminal cave peels apart the two layers of dura that floor the middle cranial fossa. This happens just lateral to where the same two layers enclose the cavernous sinus.
So the ganglion lies in a dural pocket next to the sinus, which is why cavernous sinus lesions can involve V1 and V2. (Last's p. 631)
The dura fuses with the pia at the posterior extremity of the ganglion

The dura fuses with the pia halfway along the ganglion (the anterior extremity of the cave), not at its posterior end.
Behind that point the root and the back half of the ganglion are bathed in CSF. (Last's p. 631)
The ophthalmic and maxillary divisions pass forwards in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus

The ophthalmic and maxillary divisions pass forward in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. Both are wholly sensory.
V1 leaves through the superior orbital fissure and V2 through foramen rotundum. (Last's p. 631)
The mandibular division passes forwards in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus before turning down

The mandibular division does not enter the cavernous sinus. It passes straight down from the lower part of the ganglion to foramen ovale, where the motor root joins it.
That is why V3 is spared in cavernous sinus lesions, which affect V1 and V2. (Last's p. 631)
Is the nerve of the frontonasal process

V1 is the nerve of the frontonasal process, so it supplies the derivatives of that process: forehead, upper eyelid, eye and nose.
V2 supplies the maxillary process and V3 the mandibular process of the first arch. (Last's p. 631)
Leaves the lower part of the trigeminal ganglion

V1 leaves the upper part of the trigeminal ganglion. V2 leaves the middle part and V3 the lower part.
The arrangement follows the face from top to bottom. (Last's p. 631)
Runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus above the trochlear nerve

V1 runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below the trochlear nerve.
The order from above down in the wall is III, IV, V1, V2 (with IV rising to the top anteriorly). (Last's p. 631)
Picks up sympathetic fibres from the cavernous plexus for dilator pupillae

In the cavernous sinus V1 picks up sympathetic fibres from the cavernous (internal carotid) plexus. They pass via the nasociliary and long ciliary nerves to dilator pupillae.
This is the sympathetic route to the pupil, separate from the parasympathetic route through the ciliary ganglion. (Last's p. 631)

questions.s: The tentorial (meningeal) branches of the ophthalmic nerve:
o: Arise at the anterior end of the cavernous sinus

The tentorial (meningeal) branches of V1 arise at the anterior end of the cavernous sinus and run back to supply the tentorium, the falx and the dura of the vault.
Pain from supratentorial dura is therefore referred to the forehead and orbit (V1 territory). (Last's p. 631)
Supply most of the supratentorial dura

V1 supplies all the supratentorial dura except that in the bony floor of the middle cranial fossa.
That is why supratentorial pain is felt in the forehead. Infratentorial dura is supplied mainly by upper cervical nerves and X. (Last's p. 631)
Supply the dura of the floor of the middle cranial fossa

The floor of the middle cranial fossa is the exception: it is supplied by meningeal branches of the maxillary and mandibular nerves (V2 and the nervus spinosus of V3).
The rest of the supratentorial dura is V1. (Last's p. 631)
Arise after the nerve divides into its three branches

The tentorial branches arise before V1 breaks into its three branches (lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary).
They come off the trunk in the cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 631)
The lacrimal nerve passes lateral to the tendinous ring

The lacrimal nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure lateral to (outside) the tendinous ring, together with the frontal and trochlear nerves.
All three lie outside the muscle cone. (Last's p. 631-2)
The lacrimal nerve runs along the lower part of the lateral orbital wall

The lacrimal nerve runs along the upper part of the lateral orbital wall to the lacrimal gland. The zygomatic nerve runs along the lower part.
The zygomatic nerve sends the communicating branch carrying secretomotor fibres up to the lacrimal nerve. (Last's p. 631-2)
The frontal nerve lies between the lacrimal and trochlear nerves in the superior orbital fissure

In the superior orbital fissure the frontal nerve lies between the lacrimal (lateral) and trochlear (medial) nerves, the three bunched together lateral to the tendinous ring.
"Lazy French Tarts" (lacrimal, frontal, trochlear) give the order from lateral to medial. (Last's p. 631-2)
The frontal nerve runs below levator palpebrae superioris

The frontal nerve runs forward in contact with the orbital periosteum above levator palpebrae superioris, not below it.
It divides into the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves. (Last's p. 631-2)
The supraorbital branch is larger than the supratrochlear

The frontal nerve divides into a large supraorbital and a small supratrochlear branch.
The supraorbital is the main continuation; the supratrochlear supplies a small central strip. (Last's p. 631-2)
The supraorbital nerve supplies the frontal sinus

The supraorbital nerve supplies the frontal sinus, the forehead (except a central strip) and the frontal scalp up to the vertex.
That is why frontal sinusitis causes pain referred over the forehead. (Last's p. 631-2)
The supraorbital nerve supplies the scalp back to the lambdoid suture

The supraorbital nerve supplies the scalp up to the vertex, not as far back as the lambdoid suture.
Behind the vertex the scalp is supplied by the greater occipital nerve (C2). (Last's p. 631-2)
The supratrochlear nerve extends well beyond the hairline

The supratrochlear nerve scarcely extends beyond the hairline, where the two supraorbital nerves meet.
It supplies a narrow central strip of forehead. (Last's p. 631-2)
Enters the tendinous ring between the two divisions of the oculomotor nerve

The nasociliary nerve enters the orbit within the tendinous ring, between the two divisions of III, so it lies inside the muscle cone.
Of the V1 branches, it is the only one that enters inside the ring. (Last's p. 631-2)
Crosses below the optic nerve

The nasociliary nerve crosses above the optic nerve, from lateral to medial, not below it.
It crosses with the ophthalmic artery. (Last's p. 631-2)
Runs along the medial wall below superior oblique and above medial rectus

After crossing the optic nerve, the nasociliary nerve runs forward along the medial wall of the orbit between superior oblique above and medial rectus below.
Here it gives the ethmoidal and infratrochlear nerves. (Last's p. 631-2)
Changes its name to posterior ethmoidal and then external nasal

The nasociliary nerve changes its name to anterior ethmoidal and then external nasal.
The posterior ethmoidal nerve is a side branch; it does not continue the main trunk. (Last's p. 631-2)
Lies in the roof of the middle and anterior ethmoidal air cells

The anterior ethmoidal nerve lies in the roof of the middle and anterior ethmoidal air cells and supplies their mucous membrane.
It reaches them through the anterior ethmoidal foramen. (Last's p. 631-2)
Makes a brief appearance in the anterior cranial fossa between two layers of dura

The anterior ethmoidal nerve makes a brief appearance in the anterior cranial fossa, between two layers of dura on the cribriform plate.
It is the only branch of V1 that passes through the cranial cavity in this way. (Last's p. 631-2)
Supplies the posteroinferior half of the nasal septum

The anterior ethmoidal nerve supplies the anterosuperior quadrant of the lateral nasal wall and the anterosuperior half of the septum.
The posteroinferior half of the septum is supplied by the nasopalatine nerve (V2). (Last's p. 631-2)
Enters the nose through the foramen caecum

The anterior ethmoidal nerve descends into the nose through a slit alongside the crista galli.
The foramen caecum lies in front of the crista galli and may transmit an emissary vein. (Last's p. 631-2)
The infratrochlear nerve arises just before the nasociliary enters the anterior ethmoidal foramen

The infratrochlear nerve leaves the nasociliary just before it enters the anterior ethmoidal foramen, and runs below the trochlea to the medial upper eyelid and the bridge of the nose.
Compare the supratrochlear, which comes from the frontal nerve. (Last's p. 631-2)
The posterior ethmoidal nerve arises distal to the infratrochlear nerve

The posterior ethmoidal nerve arises proximal to (before) the infratrochlear nerve, not distal to it.
It leaves through the posterior ethmoidal foramen. (Last's p. 631-2)
The posterior ethmoidal nerve does not reach the nasal cavity

The posterior ethmoidal nerve does not reach the nasal cavity. It supplies the posterior ethmoidal cells and the sphenoidal sinus, and it is often very small or absent.
The anterior ethmoidal nerve is the one that reaches the nose. (Last's p. 631-2)
The long ciliary nerves are usually four in number

The long ciliary nerves are usually two in number.
The short ciliary nerves, from the ciliary ganglion, are much more numerous (8 to 10). (Last's p. 631-2)
The communicating branch to the ciliary ganglion is its sensory root

The communicating branch from the nasociliary nerve to the ciliary ganglion is the ganglion's sensory root. Its fibres pass through the ganglion without synapse.
They then travel in the short ciliary nerves to the eyeball. (Last's p. 631-2)
There are usually 2-3 short ciliary nerves

There are 8 to 10 short ciliary nerves, not 2 to 3.
It is the long ciliary nerves that are usually two. (Last's p. 631-2)
The long ciliary nerves carry sympathetic fibres to dilator pupillae

The long ciliary nerves carry sympathetic fibres to dilator pupillae. These were picked up by the ophthalmic nerve in the cavernous sinus.
They also carry sensory fibres from the cornea and iris. (Last's p. 631-2)
The ciliary nerves supply sensation to the conjunctiva

The ciliary nerves supply the eye, including the cornea, but not the conjunctiva.
The conjunctiva is supplied by surface branches of V1 and V2 (for example the infratrochlear, lacrimal and infraorbital nerves). (Last's p. 631-2)
Is the nerve of the maxillary process of the first arch

V2 is the nerve of the maxillary process, which grows from the first pharyngeal arch.
Its territory is the middle part of the face: lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, upper teeth and palate. (Last's p. 632)
Leaves the upper part of the trigeminal ganglion

V2 leaves the middle part of the trigeminal ganglion. The ophthalmic leaves the upper part, the mandibular the lower part.
The order follows the face from top to bottom. (Last's p. 632)
Runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below the ophthalmic nerve

V2 runs forward in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below V1, then leaves through foramen rotundum.
It is the lowest nerve in the lateral wall. (Last's p. 632)
Is directed into foramen rotundum because the lateral wall fuses with dura at the medial margin of the foramen

The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus fuses with the dura at the lateral margin of foramen rotundum, which directs V2 into the foramen.
"Medial" is the changed word. (Last's p. 632)

questions.s: Concerning the maxillary nerve in the pterygopalatine fossa and orbit:
o: It enters the upper part of the pterygopalatine fossa

V2 enters the upper part of the pterygopalatine fossa through foramen rotundum.
In the fossa it gives its ganglionic branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion, the zygomatic nerve and the posterior superior alveolar nerve. (Last's p. 632)
It runs laterally for a centimetre or so in the inferior orbital fissure

V2 then runs laterally for a centimetre or so in the inferior orbital fissure, where it becomes the infraorbital nerve.
The infraorbital nerve runs forward in the floor of the orbit in its groove and canal. (Last's p. 632)
Its middle meningeal branch supplies the posterior half of the middle cranial fossa

The middle meningeal branch of V2 supplies the anterior half of the middle cranial fossa. The nervus spinosus (V3) supplies the posterior half.
Both come off before the nerves leave the skull. (Last's p. 632)
Its trunk runs just above the roof of the fossa

The trunk of V2 runs just below the roof of the pterygopalatine fossa, not above it.
The roof is formed by the body of the sphenoid and the orbit above. (Last's p. 632)

questions.s: The pterygopalatine ganglion and its connections:
o: The ganglionic branches form a single stout trunk despite their plural name

The ganglionic branches of V2 to the pterygopalatine ganglion are described in the plural but form a single stout trunk, which passes downward and medially to the ganglion.
These fibres are sensory and pass through without synapse. (Last's p. 632-3)
Most maxillary fibres pass through the ganglion into its branches

Most of the fibres of V2 pass through the ganglion into its branches (nasal, palatine, pharyngeal), mingling with the postganglionic fibres from the nerve of the pterygoid canal.
So the "branches of the ganglion" are really mostly V2 sensory fibres. (Last's p. 632-3)
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the anterosuperior half of the nasal septum

The nasopalatine nerve supplies the posteroinferior half of the nasal septum. The anterior ethmoidal nerve (V1) supplies the anterosuperior half.
The septum is thus split between V1 and V2. (Last's p. 632-3)
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the gum behind the canines

The nasopalatine nerve supplies the gum behind the two upper incisor teeth, reaching it through the incisive canal.
The palatal gum behind the canines and further back is supplied by the greater palatine nerve. (Last's p. 632-3)
The greater palatine nerve runs between the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone and the body of the maxilla

The greater palatine nerve descends in the greater palatine canal, between the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone and the body of the maxilla, and emerges on the hard palate through the greater palatine foramen.
The lesser palatine nerves descend beside it and emerge through the lesser palatine foramina to the soft palate. (Last's p. 632-3)
The greater palatine nerve supplies all the hard palate except the incisor gum

The greater palatine nerve supplies the mucosa of the hard palate from the incisor gum backwards, including the palatal gum.
The gum behind the incisors is supplied by the nasopalatine nerve through the incisive canal. (Last's p. 632-3)
The lesser palatine nerves supply only the oral surface of the soft palate

The lesser palatine nerves supply both surfaces of the soft palate and the tonsil, not just the oral surface.
They also carry taste fibres from the palate (whose cell bodies are in the geniculate ganglion). (Last's p. 632-3)
The pharyngeal branch passes through the pterygoid canal

The pharyngeal branch passes back through the palatovaginal canal to the nasopharynx.
The pterygoid canal carries the nerve of the pterygoid canal (greater and deep petrosal fibres) forward into the fossa. The two run in opposite directions. (Last's p. 632-3)

questions.s: Nerve supply of the nasal walls (Last's):
o: Posterior superior lateral and medial nasal nerves supply the posterosuperior quadrant of the lateral wall and septum

The posterior superior lateral and medial nasal nerves enter the nose through the sphenopalatine foramen and supply the posterosuperior quadrant of the lateral wall and the septum.
The anterior ethmoidal nerve supplies the anterosuperior part; the nasopalatine continues along the septum. (Last's p. 632-3)
Branches of the greater palatine nerve supply the posteroinferior quadrant of the lateral wall

Nasal branches of the greater palatine nerve supply the posteroinferior quadrant of the lateral nasal wall and the adjacent floor of the nose.
They arise as the nerve descends in the greater palatine canal. (Last's p. 632-3)
The pharyngeal branch supplies nasopharyngeal mucosa down to the soft palate's free border

The pharyngeal branch supplies the nasopharyngeal mucosa down to the level of the opening of the auditory tube, not down to the free border of the soft palate.
Below that, the pharynx is supplied by IX and X through the pharyngeal plexus. (Last's p. 632-3)
The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the posterosuperior quadrant of the lateral nasal wall

The anterior superior alveolar nerve reaches the anteroinferior quadrant of the lateral nasal wall, including the area around the nasolacrimal duct opening.
The posterosuperior quadrant is supplied by the posterior superior lateral nasal nerves. (Last's p. 632-3)
Arises from the maxillary nerve in the pterygopalatine fossa

The zygomatic nerve branches off V2 in the pterygopalatine fossa and enters the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure.
It then divides into zygomaticotemporal and zygomaticofacial branches. (Last's p. 633)
Runs along the upper part of the lateral wall of the orbit

The zygomatic nerve runs along the lower part of the lateral orbital wall. The lacrimal nerve runs along the upper part.
The two are linked by a communicating branch on that wall. (Last's p. 633)
Carries postganglionic secretomotor fibres for the lacrimal gland

The zygomatic nerve carries postganglionic secretomotor fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion. They pass up the lateral orbital wall to join the lacrimal nerve and reach the lacrimal gland.
Preganglionic fibres came from VII via the greater petrosal nerve. (Last's p. 633)
Its zygomaticotemporal branch supplies the hairy skin of the temple

The zygomaticotemporal branch supplies the hairless skin of the temple above the zygomatic arch. The hairy temporal scalp is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve (V3).
So the temple is split between V2 in front and V3 behind. (Last's p. 633)
The posterior superior alveolar nerve emerges through the pterygomaxillary fissure

The posterior superior alveolar nerve leaves the pterygopalatine fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure, usually as three branches, and runs down the back of the maxilla.
It supplies the molars, gum and maxillary sinus. (Last's p. 633)
The posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies all roots of the three molar teeth

The posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the molars except the anterior buccal (mesiobuccal) root of the first molar.
That root is supplied by the middle superior alveolar nerve, which is why anaesthesia of the first molar may need two injections. (Last's p. 633)
The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the premolars

The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the premolars and the anterior buccal root of the first molar.
It is the most variable of the superior alveolar nerves and may be absent. (Last's p. 633)
The middle superior alveolar nerve arises in the infraorbital canal

The middle superior alveolar nerve arises in the infraorbital groove. The anterior superior alveolar nerve arises in the infraorbital canal.
Groove first, canal second, from back to front. (Last's p. 633)

questions.s: The infraorbital nerve on the face:
o: Emerges between levator labii superioris and levator anguli oris

The infraorbital nerve emerges from the infraorbital foramen between levator labii superioris (in front, superficial) and levator anguli oris (behind, deep).
It then fans out to the lower eyelid, side of the nose and upper lip. (Last's p. 633)
Communicates with the facial nerve for proprioception from facial muscles

The infraorbital branches communicate with branches of VII, carrying proprioception from the facial muscles, which the facial nerve itself does not carry.
The same applies to other V branches on the face: V provides the sensory side of facial muscles. (Last's p. 633)
Its labial branches supply the upper lip and gum to the first premolar

The labial branches supply the upper lip and labial gum up to and including the gum of the second premolar, not just to the first premolar.
The same "to the second premolar" pattern applies to the mental nerve in the lower jaw. (Last's p. 633)
Its nasal branches supply the whole skin of the external nose

The nasal branches of the infraorbital nerve supply only a small strip of skin along the side of the external nose.
Much of the nose is supplied by V1 (infratrochlear and external nasal nerves). (Last's p. 633)
Leaves the inferior part of the trigeminal ganglion

V3 leaves the lower part of the trigeminal ganglion and passes straight down to foramen ovale, joined there by the motor root.
Unlike V1 and V2, it does not run in the cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 633)
Is joined by the motor root at foramen ovale

The motor root passes beneath the trigeminal ganglion and joins V3 at foramen ovale.
So V3 is the only mixed division of the trigeminal nerve. (Last's p. 633)
Divides after about 2 cm in the infratemporal fossa

Last's says V3 divides after only 4 or 5 mm in the infratemporal fossa, not 2 cm.
The short trunk gives the nervus spinosus and the nerve to medial pterygoid before dividing into anterior and posterior divisions. (Last's p. 633)
Lies between the lower head of lateral pterygoid and tensor palati

The trunk lies between the upper head of lateral pterygoid and tensor palati (tensor veli palatini), not the lower head.
The otic ganglion lies on its medial side. (Last's p. 633)
The nervus spinosus may pass through foramen ovale

The nervus spinosus (meningeal branch of V3) may pass back into the skull through foramen ovale, though classically it goes through foramen spinosum with the middle meningeal artery.
Its name comes from foramen spinosum. (Last's p. 633)
The nervus spinosus supplies the dura of the anterior half of the middle fossa

The nervus spinosus supplies the dura of the posterior half of the middle cranial fossa. The meningeal branch of the maxillary nerve supplies the anterior half.
Both are exceptions to the V1 supply of supratentorial dura. (Last's p. 633)
The nervus spinosus supplies the mastoid antrum and air cells

The nervus spinosus passes between the squamous and petrous parts of the temporal bone to supply the mastoid antrum and air cells. It is regarded as the nerve of the first pharyngeal pouch.
This links the mastoid with the dura of the middle fossa, a route for referred pain. (Last's p. 633)
The nerve to medial pterygoid enters the superficial surface of the muscle

The nerve to medial pterygoid sinks into the deep surface of the muscle, not the superficial surface.
It also sends fibres past the otic ganglion to tensor tympani and tensor palati. (Last's p. 633)
Arises from the trunk before it divides

The nerve to medial pterygoid is one of two branches from the trunk of V3 before it divides; the other is the nervus spinosus.
The anterior and posterior divisions give all the other branches. (Last's p. 633)
Supplies tensor tympani

The nerve to medial pterygoid gives a branch near (past) the otic ganglion that supplies tensor tympani.
Tensor tympani is a first-arch muscle, so it is supplied by V3, unlike stapedius (second arch, VII). (Last's p. 633)
Supplies tensor palati

The same branch from the nerve to medial pterygoid supplies tensor palati (tensor veli palatini).
It is the only palatal muscle not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. (Last's p. 633)
Relays in the otic ganglion

The nerve to medial pterygoid passes close to, or through, the otic ganglion without relaying. It is a somatic motor nerve, so it does not synapse in an autonomic ganglion.
Only parasympathetic fibres relay in the otic ganglion. (Last's p. 633)

questions.s: The anterior division of the mandibular nerve:
o: Gives two nerves to the lateral pterygoid, one to each head

The anterior division gives a nerve to each head of lateral pterygoid, two deep temporal nerves, the masseteric nerve and the buccal nerve.
All except the buccal nerve are motor. (Last's p. 634)
Gives a single deep temporal nerve

The anterior division gives two deep temporal nerves (anterior and posterior), not one.
They pass above lateral pterygoid to enter the deep surface of temporalis. (Last's p. 634)
Contains only one sensory branch, the buccal nerve

The buccal nerve is the only sensory branch of the otherwise motor anterior division.
In contrast, the posterior division is mainly sensory (auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar), with one motor branch, the nerve to mylohyoid. (Last's p. 634)
The nerve to masseter passes between the two heads of lateral pterygoid

The buccal nerve is the only nerve that passes between the two heads of lateral pterygoid. The nerve to masseter passes above the upper head, then through the mandibular notch.
The masseteric nerve also gives a twig to the temporomandibular joint. (Last's p. 634)
Supplies a thumbprint area of skin below the zygomatic bone

The buccal nerve supplies a "thumbprint" area of skin over the soft cheek below the zygomatic bone.
The rest of the cheek is supplied by the infraorbital (V2) and great auricular nerves. (Last's p. 634)
Pierces buccinator

The buccal nerve pierces buccinator and then supplies the mucous membrane on its deep surface.
It passes through the muscle without supplying it. (Last's p. 634)
Ends by supplying the vestibular gum of the mandibular premolars

The buccal nerve ends on the vestibular (buccal) gum of the three mandibular molars.
The vestibular gum of the premolars and incisors is supplied by the mental nerve. (Last's p. 634)
Is motor to buccinator

Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression supplied by VII. The buccal nerve (V3) is purely sensory.
It is the only sensory branch of the anterior division. (Last's p. 634)
Has two roots around the middle meningeal artery

The auriculotemporal nerve arises by two roots that encircle the middle meningeal artery and unite behind it.
It is therefore a landmark for finding the artery in the infratemporal fossa. (Last's p. 634)
Gives the major sensory supply to the mandibular joint

The auriculotemporal nerve is the main sensory supply of the temporomandibular joint, with a smaller contribution from the masseteric nerve.
This follows Hilton's law: nerves supplying the muscles acting on a joint also supply the joint. (Last's p. 634)
Passes in front of the neck of the mandible

The auriculotemporal nerve passes back deep to the neck of the mandible, then curves around behind it to turn upward.
This places it close to the joint and the upper parotid. (Last's p. 634)
Runs in front of the superficial temporal vessels

The temporal branch of the auriculotemporal nerve runs behind the superficial temporal vessels, not in front.
This is the order seen in front of the ear: nerve behind, artery and vein in front of it. (Last's p. 634)
Lies on medial pterygoid between the mandible and sphenomandibular ligament

The inferior alveolar nerve descends on medial pterygoid, between the ramus of the mandible and the sphenomandibular ligament, to the mandibular foramen.
This is where an inferior alveolar block is injected. (Last's p. 634)
Enters the mandibular foramen behind the inferior alveolar artery

The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen in front of the inferior alveolar artery and vein.
The vessels lie behind it. (Last's p. 634)
The nerve to mylohyoid pierces the sphenomandibular ligament

The nerve to mylohyoid leaves the inferior alveolar nerve just before the mandibular foramen and pierces the sphenomandibular ligament.
It runs in the mylohyoid groove to supply mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric. (Last's p. 634)
Supplies the posterior six teeth before dividing

Within the mandible the inferior alveolar nerve supplies the posterior five teeth (three molars and two premolars) before dividing.
It then divides into the incisive branch (canine and incisors) and the mental nerve. (Last's p. 634)

questions.s: Terminal branches of the inferior alveolar nerve:
o: The incisive branch overlaps to the opposite central incisor

The incisive branch supplies the canine and both incisors, and overlaps across the midline to the opposite central incisor.
This overlap explains why anaesthesia of a lower central incisor may need bilateral block. (Last's p. 634)
The mental nerve supplies the gum from the midline to the first premolar

The mental nerve supplies the labial gum from the midline back to and including the second premolar.
"To the second premolar" is the rule for both the upper labial gum (infraorbital) and the lower (mental). (Last's p. 634)
The mental nerve carries a few otic ganglion fibres to the labial glands

The mental nerve supplies the lower lip and labial gum, and carries a few otic ganglion secretomotor fibres to the labial glands.
This parasympathetic hitch-hiking on sensory nerves is a common pattern in the head. (Last's p. 634)
The nerve to mylohyoid is accompanied by the submental branches of the lingual artery

The nerve to mylohyoid is accompanied by the submental branches of the facial artery and vein.
The lingual artery runs deep to hyoglossus, away from the mylohyoid groove. (Last's p. 634)
Is joined by the chorda tympani about 2 cm below the skull base

The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve about 2 cm below the skull base, deep to the lower border of lateral pterygoid.
From this point the lingual nerve carries taste and secretomotor fibres. (Last's p. 634)
Curves down on medial pterygoid about 1 cm behind the inferior alveolar nerve

The lingual nerve curves down on medial pterygoid about 1 cm in front of the inferior alveolar nerve, not behind it.
So during an inferior alveolar block the lingual nerve is often anaesthetised too. (Last's p. 634)
Passes under the free lower border of the superior constrictor

The lingual nerve passes under the free lower border of the superior constrictor, then runs forward above mylohyoid into the floor of the mouth.
This places it just below and behind the third molar. (Last's p. 634)
Passes above the submandibular duct before ascending on hyoglossus

The lingual nerve dips below the submandibular duct, then ascends on hyoglossus medial to it (it "double-crosses" the duct).
On hyoglossus the order from above down is lingual nerve, duct, hypoglossal nerve. (Last's p. 634)
Supplies only half of the floor of the mouth, the rest from the mylohyoid nerve

Last's says the lingual nerve, and no other, supplies all the mucous membrane of the floor of the mouth.
The nerve to mylohyoid is motor (mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric) and gives no mucosal supply. (Last's p. 634)
Grooves the lingual plate of the mandible just below the last molar

The lingual nerve lies against the periosteum of the lingual plate just below and behind the last molar, and may groove the bone.
It is at risk in third molar extraction, giving loss of sensation and taste on that side of the tongue. (Last's p. 634)
Carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue

The lingual nerve carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, through its chorda tympani fibres.
The posterior third (and vallate papillae) is supplied by IX. (Last's p. 634)
Gives a gingival branch supplying the lingual gum to the midline

A gingival branch of the lingual nerve supplies all the lingual gum of the mandibular teeth to the midline.
The vestibular gum is split between the buccal nerve (molars) and the mental nerve (front teeth). (Last's p. 634)
The nucleus is in the lower pons

The abducent nucleus lies in the lower pons, beneath the facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
The facial fibres loop over it. (Last's p. 634-5)
The nerve contains about 66 000 fibres

The abducent nerve contains about 6600 fibres, not 66 000.
The factor of ten is the trap. Compare III (24 000) and IV (3400). (Last's p. 634-5)
It emerges at the lower border of the pons above the pyramid

VI emerges at the lower border of the pons above the pyramid, close to the midline.
It then runs up through the pontine cistern on the clivus. (Last's p. 634-5)
It pierces the dura on the clivus below the level of the jugular tubercle

VI pierces the dura on the clivus above the level of the jugular tubercle, not below.
It then runs between the dural layers to the petrous apex. (Last's p. 634-5)
Enters the inferior petrosal sinus at the apex of the petrous temporal bone

At the apex of the petrous temporal bone VI enters the inferior petrosal sinus, then bends forward under the petroclinoid ligament into the cavernous sinus.
The sharp bend over the apex is the reason for its vulnerability to raised pressure and petrous apex infection. (Last's p. 634-5)
Passes medial to the S-bend of the internal carotid in the cavernous sinus

In the cavernous sinus VI passes lateral to the S-bend of the internal carotid artery, not medial to it.
Lying free against the artery, it is often the first nerve affected by cavernous carotid aneurysms. (Last's p. 634-5)
Enters the ocular surface of lateral rectus one-third of the way along

VI enters the ocular (deep) surface of lateral rectus about one-third of the way along the muscle, like the branches of III to their muscles.
IV is the exception, entering the orbital surface of superior oblique. (Last's p. 634-5)
Enters the tendinous ring above the superior division of oculomotor

VI enters the tendinous ring below the inferior division of III, as the lowest nerve within the ring.
Within the ring from above: superior division of III, nasociliary, inferior division of III, VI. (Last's p. 634-5)
The nervus intermedius contains visceral efferent as well as afferent fibres

The nervus intermedius contains visceral efferent (secretomotor) fibres as well as afferent taste and sensory fibres. So calling it the "sensory root" of VII is not entirely appropriate.
Its efferent fibres come from the superior salivary nucleus. (Last's p. 635)
The facial nerve contains about 70 000 fibres

Last's gives the facial nerve about 7000 fibres, not 70 000.
The factor-of-ten change is the trap. (Last's p. 635)
The facial nucleus is deep in the reticular formation of the lower pons

The facial motor nucleus lies deep in the reticular formation of the lower pons, not in the ventricular floor. Its fibres loop around the abducent nucleus before emerging.
Like other branchial motor nuclei (V motor, nucleus ambiguus), it lies away from the midline and deep. (Last's p. 635)
The facial nerve fibres themselves produce the bulge of the facial colliculus

The facial colliculus is produced by the abducent nucleus lying deep to the looping facial fibres. The fibres alone do not make the bulge.
Despite the name, the colliculus is mainly the abducent nucleus. (Last's p. 635)
The secretomotor nucleus is the superior salivary nucleus

The secretomotor nucleus of VII is the superior salivary nucleus, part of the general visceral efferent column.
It supplies the lacrimal, nasal and palatal glands (via the greater petrosal) and the submandibular and sublingual glands (via the chorda tympani). (Last's p. 635)
The secretomotor nucleus is the inferior salivary nucleus

The inferior salivary nucleus belongs to IX and supplies the parotid via the otic ganglion.
Superior = VII; inferior = IX. (Last's p. 635)
Taste fibres end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius

Taste fibres of VII end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius, which lies further laterally, mostly in the medulla.
Taste fibres of IX and X end there too: it is the common taste and visceral sensory nucleus. (Last's p. 635)
Cutaneous fibres from the external ear end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius

Cutaneous fibres from the external ear carried by VII end in the trigeminal sensory nuclei, not in the tractus solitarius.
Somatic sensation in any cranial nerve goes to the trigeminal nuclei; visceral sensation and taste go to the tractus solitarius. (Last's p. 635)

questions.s: The facial nerve at the internal acoustic meatus:
o: The nervus intermedius emerges between the pons and the inferior cerebellar peduncle

The nervus intermedius emerges between the pons and the inferior cerebellar peduncle, between the facial motor root and VIII.
Its name reflects this intermediate position. (Last's p. 635)
In the meatus the facial nerve lies on the upper surface of the eighth nerve

In the internal acoustic meatus the facial nerve lies on the upper surface of VIII, with the nervus intermedius between them.
The facial nerve is therefore stretched over the surface of a vestibular schwannoma. (Last's p. 635)
The facial nerve passes into the anteroinferior quadrant of the meatus

At the fundus the facial nerve passes into the anterosuperior quadrant. The cochlear nerve occupies the anteroinferior quadrant.
"Seven up, Coke down" for the anterior quadrants; the vestibular nerves take the posterior quadrants. (Last's p. 635)
The facial nerve runs below the vestibule of the internal ear

The facial nerve runs above the vestibule of the internal ear, in the labyrinthine segment of the canal.
It passes between the cochlea and the vestibule on its way to the geniculum. (Last's p. 635)

questions.s: The facial nerve in the temporal bone:
o: The geniculum is a sharp posterior bend near the middle ear

The geniculum is a sharp bend backward near the medial wall of the middle ear, distended by the geniculate ganglion.
The greater petrosal nerve leaves here. (Last's p. 635)
It runs in the medial wall of the middle ear below the promontory

In the medial wall of the middle ear the facial canal runs above the promontory, just below the bulge of the lateral semicircular canal.
It is an important landmark in middle ear surgery. The promontory is produced by the basal turn of the cochlea. (Last's p. 635)
It passes deep to the aditus to the antrum

The facial nerve passes back deep to the aditus to the mastoid antrum, then turns down vertically in the facial canal in the posterior wall.
This is the second genu, a common site of injury in mastoid surgery. (Last's p. 635)
It emerges from the stylomastoid foramen carrying taste fibres

By the time the facial nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen it has shed all its nervus intermedius fibres (greater petrosal and chorda tympani) and is purely branchial motor.
So a lesion at the stylomastoid foramen spares taste. (Last's p. 635)
Is a branch of the nervus intermedius

The greater petrosal nerve is a branch of the nervus intermedius. Last's calls it the "nerve of tear secretion".
It carries preganglionic secretomotor fibres to the pterygopalatine ganglion and taste fibres from the palate. (Last's p. 635-6)
Has its taste fibre cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion

The cell bodies of the palatal taste fibres in the greater petrosal nerve lie in the geniculate ganglion.
These fibres pass through the pterygopalatine ganglion without synapse. (Last's p. 635-6)
Runs through the petrous bone at a 90 degree angle to the facial nerve

The greater petrosal nerve runs through the petrous bone at a 45 degree slant forward and medially from the geniculum, not at 90 degrees.
It emerges through its hiatus on the anterior surface of the petrous bone. (Last's p. 635-6)
Passes above the trigeminal ganglion

The greater petrosal nerve passes beneath the trigeminal ganglion in Meckel's cave, on its way to foramen lacerum.
This is why elevating the dura in a middle fossa approach can tug on it. (Last's p. 635-6)
The deep petrosal nerve has its cell bodies in the superior cervical ganglion

The deep petrosal nerve is made of postganglionic sympathetic fibres whose cell bodies are in the superior cervical ganglion. They peel off the internal carotid plexus.
They join the greater petrosal to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal. (Last's p. 635-6)
The secretomotor fibres relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion

In the pterygopalatine ganglion only the secretomotor (parasympathetic) fibres relay. Taste, sympathetic and maxillary sensory fibres pass straight through.
This is the general rule for all four cranial parasympathetic ganglia. (Last's p. 635-6)
Lacrimal fibres reach the gland via the nasociliary nerve

Lacrimal secretomotor fibres reach the gland via the zygomatic nerve and then a communicating branch to the lacrimal nerve.
The nasociliary nerve carries sensory fibres for the eye, not secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland. (Last's p. 635-6)
The deep petrosal nerve joins the greater petrosal at the foramen ovale

The deep petrosal nerve joins the greater petrosal nerve at foramen lacerum, forming the nerve of the pterygoid canal.
Foramen ovale transmits V3, not these nerves. (Last's p. 635-6)

questions.s: Branches of the facial nerve in the temporal bone:
o: Tympanic branches have their cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion

The tympanic (sensory) branches of VII have their cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion.
That is why herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) can produce vesicles in the external meatus and on the tympanic membrane, with facial palsy. (Last's p. 636)
The chorda tympani leaves the facial nerve 6 mm below the stylomastoid foramen

The chorda tympani leaves the facial nerve about 6 mm above the stylomastoid foramen, within the facial canal, not below it.
It then runs up and forward through the posterior wall into the middle ear. (Last's p. 636)
The chorda passes over the pars flaccida and neck of malleus

The chorda tympani passes over the pars flaccida of the tympanic membrane and the neck of the malleus, draped by mucous membrane.
It can be damaged in middle ear surgery, causing altered taste. (Last's p. 636)
The chorda tympani enters the middle ear through its anterior wall

The chorda tympani enters the middle ear through its posterior wall and leaves through the anterior wall.
It exits the skull through the petrotympanic fissure. (Last's p. 636)
Emerges at the medial end of the petrotympanic fissure

The chorda tympani leaves the skull at the medial end of the petrotympanic fissure.
It then runs down and forward towards the lingual nerve. (Last's p. 636)
Grooves the medial side of the spine of the sphenoid

On its way to the lingual nerve the chorda tympani grooves the medial side of the spine of the sphenoid.
It lies close to the middle meningeal artery and the auriculotemporal nerve here. (Last's p. 636)
Joins the lingual nerve below the lower border of lateral pterygoid

The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve just above the lower border of lateral pterygoid, about 2 cm below the skull base.
So the junction lies hidden by lateral pterygoid. (Last's p. 636)
Contains fibres from both the motor root and the nervus intermedius

All the fibres of the chorda tympani belong to the nervus intermedius: taste afferents and preganglionic secretomotor fibres. It contains no fibres from the motor root.
The motor root supplies the muscles of facial expression and other second-arch muscles. (Last's p. 636)

questions.s: Extracranial branches of the facial nerve include the nerve(s) to:
o: The occipital belly of occipitofrontalis

The posterior auricular nerve, given off just after the stylomastoid foramen, supplies the occipital belly of occipitofrontalis and the posterior auricular muscles.
The frontal belly is supplied by the temporal branches. (Last's p. 636)
The posterior belly of digastric

Before entering the parotid, VII gives a branch to the posterior belly of digastric, a second-arch muscle.
The anterior belly is first arch and supplied by V3 (nerve to mylohyoid). (Last's p. 636)
Stylohyoid

Stylohyoid is a second-arch muscle supplied by VII just after it leaves the stylomastoid foramen.
All second-arch muscles (facial muscles, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric) are VII. (Last's p. 636)
Platysma

Platysma is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the cervical branch, one of the five groups of terminal branches.
The terminal groups are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical. (Last's p. 636)
Its first neuron is bipolar with its cell body at the base of the bony spiral lamina

The first neuron of the cochlear pathway is bipolar, with its cell body in the spiral (cochlear) ganglion at the base of the bony spiral lamina.
Its peripheral process goes to the hair cells of the spiral organ. (Last's p. 636-7)
It pierces the dura at the anterosuperior quadrant of the internal meatus

The cochlear nerve pierces the dura at the anteroinferior quadrant of the fundus of the internal meatus. The facial nerve occupies the anterosuperior quadrant.
"Seven up, Coke down." (Last's p. 636-7)
The eighth nerve enters the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the lower border of the pons

VIII enters the brainstem at the lower border of the pons, at the inferior cerebellar peduncle, lateral to the facial nerve.
The cochlear nuclei lie on the surface of the peduncle there. (Last's p. 636-7)
The facial nerve lies behind the eighth nerve in the pontine cistern

In the pontine cistern the facial nerve and nervus intermedius lie in front of VIII, not behind.
They pass together to the internal acoustic meatus, VII in front and above. (Last's p. 636-7)
About 30 000 cochlear fibres relay in the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei

About 30 000 cochlear fibres relay in the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei on the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
All cochlear fibres end there, so a nuclear lesion causes ipsilateral deafness. (Last's p. 637)
Crossing fibres in the lower pons form the trapezoid body

Fibres crossing in the lower pons form the trapezoid body, then ascend as the lateral lemniscus to the inferior colliculus.
Some fibres relay in the superior olivary and trapezoid nuclei, important for localising sound. (Last's p. 637)
Cochlear representation is largely contralateral

Cochlear representation is largely bilateral above the cochlear nuclei.
That is why a unilateral lesion of the lateral lemniscus or auditory cortex does not cause deafness in one ear. (Last's p. 637)
The auditory radiation passes through the retrolentiform internal capsule

The auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule. The optic radiation is retrolentiform.
"Auditory below, visual behind." (Last's p. 637)
The inferior colliculus relays for reflex effects of sound

The inferior colliculus is a relay for reflex effects of sound (turning the head and eyes to a noise) through the tectobulbar and tectospinal tracts.
It also relays fibres to the medial geniculate body for conscious hearing. (Last's p. 637)
The medial geniculate body is a displaced hypothalamic nucleus

The medial geniculate body is a displaced thalamic nucleus, though anatomically it lies in the midbrain. It is not hypothalamic.
It relays auditory impulses to the auditory cortex. (Last's p. 637)
The auditory cortex lies below and within the lateral sulcus

The primary auditory cortex (areas 41 and 42) lies on the transverse temporal gyri, hidden below and within the lateral sulcus.
The surrounding auditory association area includes Wernicke's area in the dominant hemisphere. (Last's p. 637)
The pathway always has exactly three neurons

The auditory pathway may have more than three neurons, since the trapezoid body and lateral lemniscus contain cell bodies where some fibres relay.
So "always exactly three" is wrong. The direct path is cochlear nucleus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate body. (Last's p. 637)
The maculae of utricle and saccule serve static balance

The maculae of the utricle and saccule respond to gravity and linear acceleration, serving static balance (head position).
The ampullae of the semicircular ducts respond to angular acceleration and serve kinetic balance. (Last's p. 637)
The nerve from the saccule emerges through the posterosuperior quadrant of the fundus

The nerve from the saccule emerges through the posteroinferior quadrant of the fundus. The posterosuperior quadrant carries fibres from the utricle and the anterior and lateral ampullae.
The posterior ampullary nerve has its own small foramen singulare. (Last's p. 637)
The posterior ampullary nerve passes through the foramen singulare

The nerve from the ampulla of the posterior semicircular duct passes through its own small opening, the foramen singulare.
This nerve can be cut (singular neurectomy) for benign positional vertigo. (Last's p. 637)
The vestibular nerve contains about 30 000 fibres

The vestibular nerve contains about 18 000 fibres. The cochlear nerve has about 30 000.
The cochlear part is the larger. (Last's p. 637)
The vestibular nuclei lie in the lateral angle of the fourth ventricle

The vestibular nuclei lie in the lateral angle of the floor of the fourth ventricle, in both pons and medulla (the vestibular area).
Four nuclei are described: superior, lateral, medial and inferior. (Last's p. 637)
They connect with the archaeocerebellum

The vestibular nuclei connect with the archaeocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe), which is concerned with balance.
Some vestibular fibres go there directly without relaying in the nuclei. (Last's p. 637)
The vestibulospinal tract arises from the medial vestibular nucleus

The vestibulospinal tract arises from the lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters' nucleus).
The medial nucleus mainly projects through the medial longitudinal fasciculus to the eye muscle nuclei and upper cord. (Last's p. 637)
Cortical connections relay through the lateral geniculate body

Last's says cortical vestibular connections relay bilaterally through the medial geniculate body to the auditory region.
The lateral geniculate body is the visual relay. (Last's p. 637)
Is the nerve of the third branchial arch

IX is the nerve of the third pharyngeal (branchial) arch. It supplies the third-arch muscle, stylopharyngeus, and the third-arch part of the tongue mucosa (posterior third).
V is the first arch, VII the second, X the fourth and sixth. (Last's p. 637)
Its branchial motor fibres supply only stylopharyngeus

The branchial motor fibres of IX come from the nucleus ambiguus and supply only stylopharyngeus.
The rest of the nucleus ambiguus supplies pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles through X. (Last's p. 637)
Its secretomotor fibres arise from the superior salivary nucleus

The secretomotor fibres of IX arise from the inferior salivary nucleus, which lies rostral to the dorsal nucleus of the vagus.
The superior salivary nucleus belongs to VII. (Last's p. 637)
Ordinary sensation from the tongue and pharynx enters the nucleus of the tractus solitarius

Last's says ordinary (general) sensation from the tongue and pharynx carried by IX enters the trigeminal sensory nuclei. Taste and carotid sinus afferents enter the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
The rule: somatic-type sensation goes to the trigeminal nuclei; taste and visceral reflex afferents go to the tractus solitarius. (Last's p. 637)

questions.s: At the jugular foramen the glossopharyngeal nerve:
o: Enters the anterior compartment

IX passes through the anterior compartment of the jugular foramen, together with the inferior petrosal sinus.
X and XI pass through the middle compartment, and the jugular bulb occupies the posterior compartment. (Last's p. 637)
Lies medial to the inferior petrosal sinus

IX lies lateral to the inferior petrosal sinus, not medial.
The sinus is the most medial structure in the foramen. (Last's p. 637)
Is separated from the vagus and accessory by a fibrous dural septum

A septum of fibrous dura separates IX (and the inferior petrosal sinus) from X and XI in the middle compartment.
So IX has its own dural sheath while X and XI share one. (Last's p. 637)
Notches the inferior border of the petrous bone above the internal acoustic meatus

IX notches the inferior border of the petrous bone just below the internal acoustic meatus, not above it.
The notch lodges its superior ganglion. (Last's p. 637)
The tympanic branch passes through the tympanic canaliculus

The tympanic branch of IX passes through the tympanic canaliculus into the middle ear, where it forms the tympanic plexus on the promontory.
It continues as the lesser petrosal nerve. (Last's p. 637-8)
The lesser petrosal nerve may leave through the petrosal foramen

The lesser petrosal nerve may leave the skull through the small petrosal foramen, or otherwise through foramen ovale, to reach the otic ganglion.
It carries preganglionic fibres for the parotid. (Last's p. 637-8)
Its pharyngeal branches are motor to the constrictors

The pharyngeal branches of IX are afferent (sensory to pharyngeal mucosa, the afferent limb of the gag reflex), not motor.
The constrictors are supplied by X through the pharyngeal plexus. (Last's p. 637-8)
It has two muscular branches

IX has only one muscular branch, the nerve to stylopharyngeus.
That is the only muscle derived from the third arch. (Last's p. 637-8)
The nucleus ambiguus supplies all the skeletal muscle supplied by the vagus

The nucleus ambiguus supplies all the skeletal muscle supplied by the vagus: pharynx, upper oesophagus, larynx and palate.
It also gives the fibres of the cranial accessory root and the motor fibres of IX to stylopharyngeus. (Last's p. 638)
The dorsal motor nucleus lies beneath the hypoglossal trigone

The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus lies beneath the vagal trigone, lateral to the hypoglossal trigone.
The hypoglossal nucleus lies beneath the hypoglossal trigone, nearest the midline. (Last's p. 638)
The dorsal motor nucleus supplies cardiac and smooth muscle

The dorsal motor nucleus supplies parasympathetic fibres to cardiac muscle and the smooth muscle and glands of the bronchi and gut.
Skeletal muscle is supplied by the nucleus ambiguus instead. (Last's p. 638)
The nucleus of the tractus solitarius receives the auricular branch fibres

The skin fibres of the auricular branch go to the trigeminal sensory nuclei.
The nucleus of the tractus solitarius receives taste and visceral afferents, not cutaneous ones. (Last's p. 638)

questions.s: The vagus at the skull base:
o: Its rootlets lie between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle

The vagal rootlets emerge in the groove between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle, below those of IX and above those of the cranial accessory.
IX, X and the cranial XI form a continuous line of rootlets. (Last's p. 638)
It lies lateral to the accessory nerve in the jugular foramen

In the jugular foramen the vagus lies medial to the accessory nerve, not lateral to it.
XI is in the lateral part of the middle compartment. (Last's p. 638)
It passes behind the jugular tubercle

The vagus passes behind the jugular tubercle on the basiocciput on its way to the jugular foramen.
So does XI; the tubercle is a landmark in far lateral approaches. (Last's p. 638)
The superior ganglion lodges cell bodies of the laryngeal sensory fibres

The superior ganglion holds only the cell bodies for the meningeal and auricular branches. Laryngeal and other sensory fibres have their cell bodies in the inferior ganglion.
Superior = somatic; inferior = visceral (and taste). (Last's p. 638)
The pharyngeal branch passes between the internal and external carotid arteries

The pharyngeal branch of X passes forward between the internal and external carotid arteries to the pharyngeal plexus. It carries both motor and sensory fibres.
It is the main motor nerve of the pharynx and soft palate. (Last's p. 638)
The superior laryngeal nerve passes superficial to the carotids

The superior laryngeal nerve runs deep to (medial to) the carotid arteries, not superficial.
It divides into internal and external laryngeal nerves behind the arteries. (Last's p. 638)
The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane

The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal vessels to supply the mucosa above the vocal folds.
It is sensory and secretomotor, the afferent limb of the cough reflex above the cords. (Last's p. 638)
The internal laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid

Cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve. The internal laryngeal nerve is sensory to pharyngeal and laryngeal mucosa.
External = motor (cricothyroid); internal = sensory. (Last's p. 638)
The right hooks under the subclavian artery

The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery in the root of the neck.
The right sixth-arch artery disappears, so the nerve rises to the next arch, the fourth (subclavian). (Last's p. 638)
The left hooks round the ligamentum arteriosum

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch of the aorta at the ligamentum arteriosum, giving it a longer course through the thorax.
That is why it is more often affected by thoracic disease, such as aortic aneurysm or lung cancer. (Last's p. 638)
They pass under the inferior constrictor just in front of the cricothyroid joint

The recurrent laryngeal nerves pass under the lower border of the inferior constrictor just behind the cricothyroid joint.
The joint is a useful landmark for finding the nerve in thyroid surgery. (Last's p. 638)
They supply laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds

The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply laryngeal mucosa below the vocal folds. Above the folds it is the internal laryngeal nerve.
The vocal folds mark the boundary. (Last's p. 638)

questions.s: Vagal sensory and motor supply of the viscera:
o: Vagal branches to the gut do not carry pain fibres

Vagal branches to the gut do not carry pain fibres. Visceral pain from the gut runs with sympathetic fibres to the thoracic and lumbar cord.
That is why abdominal visceral pain is referred to dermatomes T5 to L1. (Last's p. 638)
The vagus carries no pain from any viscera

Last's says the vagus is sensory to the thoracic viscera: oesophagus, trachea and lungs. So it does carry some visceral sensation, including from those structures.
The point is that vagal branches to the abdominal gut do not carry pain. (Last's p. 638)
The vagal trunks enter the abdomen through the oesophageal opening
