The anterior and posterior vagal trunks form from the oesophageal plexus and pass through the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm.
The anterior trunk is mainly from the left vagus, the posterior from the right (from the rotation of the gut). (Last's p. 638)
The vagal trunks supply the stomach from branches in the greater omentum

The vagal trunks supply the stomach through branches that arise in the lesser omentum (along the lesser curvature, the nerves of Latarjet).
This is the basis of highly selective vagotomy. (Last's p. 638)
The cranial root gives all its fibres to the vagus

The cranial root of the accessory nerve, from the nucleus ambiguus, gives all its fibres to the vagus.
It is really an aberrant part of the vagus. (Last's p. 639)
The spinal root arises from the anterior horn of the upper two segments only

The spinal root arises from the anterior horn of the upper five or six cervical segments (mainly C2, 3 and 4), not just the upper two.
Its rootlets join and ascend through the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 639)
Spinal accessory rootlets emerge behind the denticulate ligament

The spinal accessory rootlets emerge from the lateral surface of the cord behind the denticulate ligament.
Anterior roots lie in front of the ligament; posterior roots and XI lie behind. (Last's p. 639)
The spinal root passes under the upper tooth of the denticulate ligament

The spinal root passes over (superficial to) the upper tooth of the denticulate ligament, not under it.
It then enters the skull through the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 639)

questions.s: The accessory nerve in the jugular foramen and neck:
o: It passes through the lateral part of the middle compartment

XI passes through the lateral part of the middle compartment of the jugular foramen, lateral to the vagus.
They share a dural sheath there. (Last's p. 639)
It lies just behind the jugular bulb

X and XI lie just in front of the jugular bulb, not behind it.
The bulb occupies the posterior compartment. (Last's p. 639)
It lies on the internal jugular vein over the lateral mass of the atlas

Below the skull XI crosses the internal jugular vein over the lateral mass (transverse process) of the atlas.
The transverse process of the atlas can be felt between the mastoid and the angle of the mandible, a landmark for finding the nerve. (Last's p. 639)
In the posterior triangle it descends over scalenus medius

In the posterior triangle XI descends over levator scapulae, not scalenus medius.
It lies within the fascia of the roof, superficial and vulnerable. (Last's p. 639)

questions.s: The cranial root of the accessory nerve:
o: Joins the spinal root in the posterior triangle

The cranial and spinal roots join only briefly to pass through the jugular foramen. The cranial root then joins the vagus.
They do not travel together in the posterior triangle; only the spinal root goes there. (Last's p. 639)
Is effectively the motor root of the vagus

The cranial root is effectively the motor root of the vagus to striated muscle (pharynx, larynx, palate).
Its fibres come from the nucleus ambiguus. (Last's p. 639)
Supplies sternocleidomastoid

Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius are supplied by the spinal root.
The cranial root supplies no muscles in the neck in its own right. (Last's p. 639)
Is analogous to the motor root of the trigeminal nerve

Just as the trigeminal motor root joins the sensory root beyond the ganglion at foramen ovale, the cranial accessory root joins the vagus distal to its ganglion.
Both are separate motor rootlets that join a sensory nerve below its ganglion. (Last's p. 639)
Its nucleus lies against the midline in the hypoglossal trigone

The hypoglossal nucleus lies against the midline in the floor of the fourth ventricle, beneath the hypoglossal trigone. It is a somatic motor nucleus.
Somatic motor nuclei (III, IV, VI, XII) all lie near the midline. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its rootlets emerge between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle

The hypoglossal rootlets emerge between the pyramid and the olive (the anterolateral sulcus).
IX, X and XI emerge behind the olive. (Last's p. 639-40)
It forms two roots in the canal, separated by a flange of dura that may ossify

XII forms two roots in the hypoglossal canal, separated by a flange of dura that sometimes ossifies to give a double canal.
The roots unite within the canal. (Last's p. 639-40)
It passes below the atlanto-occipital joint in the canal

In the canal the nerve passes forward above the atlanto-occipital joint, not below.
The canal lies above the occipital condyle. (Last's p. 639-40)
Spirals behind the inferior ganglion of the vagus

After leaving the canal XII spirals behind the inferior ganglion of the vagus, then comes forward behind and around the carotid arteries.
It is bound to the vagus here by connective tissue. (Last's p. 639-40)
Lies on the occipital, internal carotid and lingual arteries below digastric

Below digastric, XII lies on the occipital, external carotid and lingual arteries, not the internal carotid.
It crosses the internal carotid higher up. (Last's p. 639-40)
Is covered only by the facial vein beneath the investing fascia here

Below the posterior belly of digastric XII is covered only by the facial vein beneath the investing fascia, so it lies very near the skin.
That superficial position puts it at risk in submandibular and carotid surgery. (Last's p. 639-40)
Passes forward on hyoglossus superficial to mylohyoid

XII passes forward on hyoglossus deep to mylohyoid, in the mouth (floor of the mouth).
It lies below the submandibular duct and lingual nerve. (Last's p. 639-40)
Branches before the tongue are all from C1 fibres

All branches of XII before it reaches the tongue are made of C1 fibres that joined it as it left the skull.
XII itself supplies only tongue muscles. (Last's p. 639-40)
The meningeal branch supplies dura of the anterior cranial fossa

The meningeal branch (C1 fibres) supplies a ring of dura in the posterior cranial fossa around the foramen magnum.
The anterior cranial fossa dura is supplied by V1 (anterior ethmoidal and others). (Last's p. 639-40)
The nerve to thyrohyoid arises as the nerve lies on the lingual artery

The nerve to thyrohyoid (C1 fibres) arises as XII lies on the lingual artery above the greater horn of the hyoid.
It runs down to thyrohyoid. (Last's p. 639-40)
The nerve to geniohyoid arises below mylohyoid

The nerve to geniohyoid is given off in the mouth, above mylohyoid.
Geniohyoid lies above mylohyoid, so its nerve leaves XII in the floor of the mouth. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its upper root branches off as the hypoglossal curves between the ICA and IJV

The upper (superior) root of the ansa cervicalis branches off XII as it curves between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein. It was formerly called the descendens hypoglossi.
It carries C1 fibres. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its lower root comes from C3 and C4

The lower (inferior) root of the ansa comes from C2 and C3, not C3 and C4.
C3 and C4 (with C5) form the phrenic nerve. (Last's p. 639-40)
It lies in the anterior wall of the carotid sheath

The ansa cervicalis lies in (or on) the anterior wall of the carotid sheath, on the internal jugular vein under sternocleidomastoid.
It supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles. (Last's p. 639-40)
Sternothyroid receives C1, C2 and C3

Sternothyroid receives C2 and C3. Sternohyoid and omohyoid receive C1, C2 and C3.
Thyrohyoid and geniohyoid get C1 alone, through XII. (Last's p. 639-40)
The nerves most commonly affected by trauma include I, II, III, VI and VII

Last's lists I, II, III, VI and VII as the cranial nerves most often affected by trauma.
I by shearing at the cribriform plate, VI by stretching over the petrous apex, VII by temporal bone fractures. (Last's p. 639-40)
Olfactory filaments are torn at the cribriform plate in anterior fossa fractures

In anterior fossa fractures the olfactory filaments are torn where they cross the cribriform plate, causing anosmia.
The same fracture may tear the meningeal sleeves and cause CSF rhinorrhoea. (Last's p. 639-40)
Most deficiencies of smell are due to olfactory nerve injury

Most loss of smell is due to disease of the nasal mucosa (colds, rhinitis, polyps), not to injury of the olfactory nerves.
Nerve injury is a less common cause. (Last's p. 639-40)
Trochlear palsy is the commonest cranial nerve lesion

Facial nerve paralysis is the commonest cranial nerve lesion.
Trochlear palsy is a recognised result of head injury but is much less common. (Last's p. 639-40)

questions.s: Branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve include:
o: The carotid sinus nerve

The carotid sinus nerve, a branch of IX, carries baroreceptor (carotid sinus) and chemoreceptor (carotid body) afferents to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
It is the afferent limb of the carotid sinus reflex. (Last's p. 639-40)
A tympanic branch

The tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve) supplies the middle ear and forms the tympanic plexus, continuing as the lesser petrosal nerve.
This is the route of referred earache from the throat. (Last's p. 639-40)
A lingual branch

The lingual branch of IX gives taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, including the vallate papillae.
The anterior two-thirds is VII (taste) and V3 (general). (Last's p. 639-40)
A tonsillar branch

Tonsillar branches of IX supply the mucosa over the palatine tonsil.
Pain after tonsillectomy is often felt in the ear because IX also supplies the middle ear through its tympanic branch. (Last's p. 639-40)

questions.s: The facial nerve and its branches (Last's):
o: Taste from the soft palate travels in the greater petrosal nerve

Taste from the soft palate travels in the greater petrosal nerve (via the palatine nerves and the pterygopalatine ganglion, without synapse).
Taste from the anterior tongue travels in the chorda tympani. Both have cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion. (Last's p. 639-40)
Tympanic branches carry somatic sensation from the tympanic membrane

Tympanic branches of VII carry somatic sensation from part of the tympanic membrane, via the tympanic plexus.
This is why geniculate herpes can produce vesicles on the drum. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its somatic afferents end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius

The somatic afferents of VII end in the trigeminal sensory nuclei.
Only taste and visceral afferents end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius. (Last's p. 639-40)
The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve about 4 cm below the skull

The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve about 2 cm below the skull, not 4 cm.
The junction lies just above the lower border of lateral pterygoid. (Last's p. 639-40)
The vagal trigone overlies the dorsal motor nucleus

The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus lies beneath the vagal trigone in the floor of the fourth ventricle, lateral to the hypoglossal trigone.
The vestibular area lies further lateral. (Last's p. 639-40)
The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply all laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid

The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply all the intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
So recurrent nerve damage paralyses posterior cricoarytenoid, the only abductor of the cords. (Last's p. 639-40)
The accessory gives its nucleus ambiguus fibres to the vagus inside the skull

The accessory gives its nucleus ambiguus fibres to the vagus outside the skull, at the inferior vagal ganglion.
Inside the skull the cranial and spinal roots travel together to the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 639-40)
The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply mucosa above the vocal folds

The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply mucosa below the vocal folds. Above the folds is the internal laryngeal nerve.
The vocal folds divide the two sensory territories. (Last's p. 639-40)
It runs superficial to the occipital and lingual arteries

XII spirals forward superficial to the internal and external carotid arteries, the occipital artery and the lingual artery.
So it is at risk in carotid endarterectomy. (Last's p. 639-40)
It runs deep to the facial vein

XII runs deep to the veins, including the facial vein, as it crosses to the tongue.
Arteries deep to the nerve, veins superficial to it. (Last's p. 639-40)
It runs deep to the internal and external carotid arteries

XII runs superficial (lateral) to the internal and external carotid arteries, not deep to them.
That is why it is seen crossing the arteries in carotid surgery. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its two roots unite outside the canal

The two roots of XII unite inside the hypoglossal canal, above the atlanto-occipital joint, not outside it.
A dural flange separates them in the canal and may ossify. (Last's p. 639-40)
